title: Why Does Weed Feel Stronger Sometimes?
h1: When a Familiar Product Hits Harder: What's Going On
metaDescription: Why does weed feel stronger sometimes? What THC percentages measure, why higher THC isn't always stronger, and how dose, format, tolerance and setting matter.
excerpt: Same product, different night, much stronger effect? Here's what potency numbers really measure and the everyday factors that can make cannabis hit harder than you expect.

body:
Why does weed feel stronger sometimes, even when it's a product you've used before? The short answer is that the number on the label tells you how much THC is in the product, not how strong your experience will be. How much you take, how you take it, your tolerance and even last night's sleep all change the result. Here's what potency numbers measure, why they don't predict intensity and how to keep sessions steady.

## Why does weed feel stronger sometimes? Start with what potency measures

So what does a THC percentage mean? It's a concentration: the share of a product's weight that's THC. Flower labeled 20% THC holds about 200 mg of THC in each gram. Edibles and drinks list milligrams instead, both for a single serving and for the whole package.

Concentration and intensity aren't the same thing. Two people can share the same 20% flower and feel completely different, and the same person can feel different from one night to the next. The label tells you what's in the jar. Everything else shapes how much THC reaches your brain and how you respond to it.

Even the number has some wiggle room. Michigan labels list THC and CBD content along with a statement that actual values may vary by 10%.

## Cannabis potency explained: how labs calculate THC in flower

Raw flower holds very little THC. Most of it is THCA, an acid form that turns into THC when heated. Labs therefore report total THC with a standard formula:

> **Total THC = THC + (THCA × 0.877)**

The 0.877 factor accounts for the extra weight of the acid group that THCA sheds when it converts. Flower testing at 24% THCA and 1% THC works out to about 22% total THC, not 25%.

Each label also reflects the batch that was tested, and the same strain name can test differently from one harvest to the next. Our guide to [reading a cannabis label](/blog/how-to-read-a-cannabis-label/) walks through the rest of the panel. For typical ranges, see our explainer on [what counts as high THC](/blog/what-is-considered-high-thc/).

## Does higher THC mean stronger? Not always

It seems logical that 30% flower should hit harder than 20%, but research on regular users complicates that. In a 2020 study published in JAMA Psychiatry, regular flower users were randomly assigned 16% or 24% THC flower, and regular concentrate users got 70% or 90% concentrates. Concentrate users ended up with much higher THC in their blood. Yet the researchers saw no differences in outcomes by product type or by potency within a type, and memory and balance were affected similarly across the groups.

There's an important caveat. These were experienced users who used as much as they wanted, so they could adjust as they went. A newer consumer, or anyone taking a fixed amount of something unfamiliar, can still get far more THC from a stronger product than they expect. Higher THC raises the ceiling, and your habits decide how close you get to it.

## Product type and onset

The way you take cannabis sets both its speed and its staying power. A 2003 review of cannabinoid pharmacology summed up the pattern:

| | Inhaled | Swallowed |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Effects begin | Within seconds to a few minutes | After 30 to 90 minutes |
| Peak | 15 to 30 minutes | 2 to 3 hours |
| How long they last | Taper off within 2 to 3 hours | About 4 to 12 hours |

That delay is why so many people find edibles stronger than expected. When nothing seems to happen, it's tempting to take more, and then both doses arrive together. Our guide to [THC drinks versus edibles](/blog/thc-drinks-vs-edibles-timing/) compares onset for drinks too.

## Dose and serving size

Dose is the most direct lever on intensity. With flower, your dose depends on how deeply and how often you inhale, and one 2005 review of cannabinoid pharmacokinetics calls smoking a highly individual process. Concentrates pack far more THC into each inhale, which is why concentrate users in the 2020 study ended up with much higher blood THC than flower users.

Edibles make dose easier to see, as long as you read both numbers on the package. In Michigan, an adult-use edible serving is capped at 10 mg of THC, and a package can hold up to 200 mg. Medical edibles can contain up to 50 mg per serving, so don't mix the two up. Eating a second piece before the first has peaked is an easy way to double a dose without meaning to. Our [THC dosage guide](/blog/thc-dosage-guide/) offers sensible starting points.

## Inhaled versus ingested: why edibles can feel stronger

Edibles aren't just slower. They can feel different, and often stronger, because of the liver. Swallowed THC is absorbed through your gut and passes through the liver before reaching the rest of your body. Only a small and variable share, roughly 4% to 12%, makes it into the bloodstream, but the liver also turns THC into 11-hydroxy-THC, an active compound.

That same 2005 review found that 11-hydroxy-THC reaches about 20% of THC levels after inhaling, but about the same level as THC itself after swallowing. That extra active compound, plus slow absorption, is one reason an edible can feel longer and heavier than the same THC inhaled. Absorption also varies widely between people, so one edible can land differently for two friends.

## Tolerance after a break, and other tolerance shifts

Regular use dulls the response. In a small 2016 brain-imaging study, 11 men with cannabis dependence had about 15% fewer available CB1 receptors, THC's main target, than people who didn't use cannabis.

That change reverses quickly once you stop. In the same study, the difference was no longer detectable after just two days without cannabis, and it was still gone at four weeks. So if you take a break and come back to your old amount, it can feel much stronger than you remember. Restart at a lower dose, and see our guide to [tolerance breaks](/blog/t-breaks-marijuana-tolerance/) for planning one.

## Body chemistry, food, sleep, setting and expectations

Plenty of everyday factors shift how a session feels, and most are less studied than potency:

- **Body chemistry.** People absorb and process THC differently, especially when it's swallowed.
- **Food and drink.** What's in your stomach can change how quickly an edible kicks in, and alcohol adds its own effects on top of cannabis.
- **Sleep and stress.** Being tired, run-down or anxious can make a familiar dose feel bigger.
- **Setting.** A calm, familiar place usually feels easier than a crowded or unfamiliar one.
- **Expectations.** If you're braced for a strong high, you may notice every sensation more.

Keeping notes on dose, time, food and mood is the simplest way to learn your own patterns.

## Tips for steadier sessions, and what to do if it's too much

For steadier sessions:

1. Start low, especially with a new product or after a break.
2. With edibles, wait at least two hours before taking more.
3. Stick with one format at a time instead of stacking an edible on top of a vape.
4. Check the serving size and the package total before you start.
5. Buy from licensed stores, where products are tested and labeled.
6. Keep notes on what worked and what didn't.

If it's too much, remember that the feeling will pass. Find a calm, quiet spot, sip water, have a snack and rest. Inhaled effects usually fade within a few hours, while an edible can last much longer. The National Poison Control Center, whose number (1-800-222-1222) appears on Michigan cannabis labels, can give advice. If someone has chest pain, trouble breathing, fainting or severe confusion, call 911. Our guide to [coming down from a high](/blog/getting-unhigh/) has more ideas.

Questions about a label? Ask a budtender at your High Society store. 21+ only. Please consume responsibly.

faq.q: Why did my weed hit harder than usual tonight?
faq.a: There are a few likely reasons: a batch that tested higher, a bigger dose than you realized, a break that lowered your tolerance, or an empty stomach, short sleep or stress. Check the label, since the same strain name can test differently from harvest to harvest. Next time, start with a smaller amount and note what was different about the night.

faq.q: Is 30% THC flower always stronger than 20%?
faq.a: Not always. The 30% flower holds more THC per gram, but how strong it feels depends on how much you inhale, your tolerance and your setting. In a 2020 study, regular users given 24% flower didn't show different effects from those given 16% flower. Newer consumers should still approach higher numbers with care and take smaller amounts.

faq.q: Why do edibles catch people off guard?
faq.a: Because they're slow. Swallowed THC can take 30 to 90 minutes to start and two to three hours to peak, so people often take more before the first dose arrives. The liver also turns THC into 11-hydroxy-THC, an active compound that builds up far more after eating than after inhaling. Start low and wait at least two hours.

faq.q: Does tolerance drop after time off?
faq.a: Yes, and the change can start quickly. In a small 2016 brain-imaging study, men with cannabis dependence had fewer available CB1 receptors than non-users, but the difference was no longer detectable after two days without cannabis and was still gone at four weeks. Coming back to your old dose after a break can feel much stronger, so restart lower.

Licensed products are tested by a lab, and the label must list the THC and CBD content, the testing lab and the test date, along with a note that actual values may vary by 10%. For flower, lab results account for THCA, the form that becomes THC when heated. Every product on our shelves has passed Michigan testing.
